name: Chloe Garcia

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Hi Chloe, thanks for talking with me. I'm a field researcher with the Work Futures Panel, an independent research group with no ties to AI companies, employers, unions, parties or government. What you tell me stays confidential, so you can say what you'd say in public and what you really think. To start, can you walk me through a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I'm a buyer at Lumen Beauty Wholesale in Rivermouth. We supply salons and barbers with hair colour, shampoo, nail products and tools. I get in around eight, check what salons ordered, and use AI tools to forecast what we'll need and compare supplier prices. Then I ring suppliers, negotiate, and write up the orders for Marguerite, the head buyer, to approve. I started in sales at a salon and moved into buying three years ago.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thanks. What do you like about it, and what wears you out?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I love the trend side, spotting that a certain hair product is about to take off, and I like the tools that make me quicker. What wears me out is the pressure to hit numbers with less budget every quarter. At home there's Dev, who's a self-employed electrician, and our kids, Zara and Ollie. It's lively, and the money is always a bit stretched.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say fine, I'm using it already and it saves me time. I'd tell my team it's a tool, not a miracle, and we should keep using what works. Online I'd skip the debate, honestly, nobody changes their mind.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honest take, it would be a bit of a relief, but my situation doesn't change. Dev's electrician work comes in lumps, some months great and some months nothing, and my pay is the steady part. Lumen's had a flat year, so I'm the one on lower pay whose job could be squeezed even without AI.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep using it daily, for trend research, supplier emails and sales forecasts. I'd use the time to get better at the part machines don't do, like winning a better deal from a supplier over a coffee. I'd put aside two hundred a month in a rainy-day account for Dev's slow months.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Fine, with a little tightness. I don't lie awake, but I do check Dev's invoices page more than I should. It's like watching a pot, hoping it doesn't boil over.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said Dev's income comes in lumps. How does that shape your decisions?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I can't take risks with my job. Last winter he had three quiet weeks and we ate through the little we had saved. Since then I treat my pay as the floor under the house.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does a better deal over coffee look like in your job?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I met the rep from a hair dye brand last month and got ten percent off a pallet because I promised a bigger order in spring. A tool can compare prices, but it can't make a promise and shake a hand. That's the human part I'm trying to be good at.

I'd tell my team it's a tool, not a **miracle**.
think: It would be a relief, but my **situation** doesn't change.
My partner's electrician income comes in **lumps**, so my pay is the steady part.
Lumen had a flat year, so my job could be squeezed even without **AI**.
do: Keep using AI daily for trend research, supplier emails and **forecasts**.
Spend the saved time winning better **deals** from suppliers face to face.
Put two hundred a month in a rainy-day **account** for my partner's slow months.

S0.quote: A tool can compare prices, but it can't make a promise and shake a hand.
fieldNote: Already an **AI user**, so a plateau costs her little but doesn't remove her money pressures.

Sees face-to-face **negotiation** as her human edge.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many thinking tasks in many jobs: writing, checking, planning, buying, booking, coding and answering customers. Robots spread into hands-on work more slowly. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. Most people still have work, and there is some time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's real and I'd say I'm already living it. At work I'd offer to write the how-to for our team, because I use the tools every day. Online I'd probably share tips, and say that the people who adapt first still need a safety net.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly, I'm ahead of most, and I'm still a junior. Buying is on the list, and if Lumen needs two buyers instead of five, they'll choose on cost. I'm cheaper than Marguerite, which helps, but cheap isn't the same as safe.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd take on the AI side of the team, run the weekly forecast with the tools and show the numbers to Marguerite. I'd ask for a new title and a raise before the layoffs, not after. And in the evenings I'd set up a small side service for independent salons, helping them pick products and prices, with ten salons as the goal for year one.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Buzzing and nervous at once. I like that I'm early, but I feel the clock. If I'm wrong about who they keep, we lose the steady pay.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make you wrong about who they keep?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If Lumen gets one clever system and one senior buyer, and no juniors at all. They might see my skills as already inside the tool and not need me. I'm learning that being good with the tools makes me useful and also replaceable.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What happens at home if your pay stopped?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Dev's lumpy income wouldn't carry the mortgage, so we'd rely on his mum for a month or two and cut the kids' phone plans. I'd take any contract work I could find, even data labelling. Zara is fourteen and she'd notice when I stopped buying her new trainers.

steps.text: Run the weekly sales forecast with AI and show Marguerite the numbers

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2031. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say it's going to be messy and fast, and people need to prepare. At work I'd tell everyone that being good with the tools won't be enough. And I'd say governments need to talk about income support now, not in 2028.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: My job is gone. When AI does the thinking part cheaper and better, the human part left is small. Dev's trade lasts longer, which is good, but his income is lumpy and the mortgage is not.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Straight away I'd do three things. One, go all in on the side business for independent salons, because small owners will still want a person. Two, look at jobs that are hands-on and with people, like a salon manager role or training roles, because robots take another three years. Three, cut hard: eating out, subscriptions and the new kitchen plan.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Alarmed but moving. It's like being on a bus that's braking too late, so you grab the pole and decide where you'd jump. I'd rather act than freeze.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The hands-on three-year gap. Does it help you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A little. A salon manager job could keep me in beauty until 2031 or so, but it's a bridge, not a place to live. It pays less than buying and I'd be starting low.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Zara and Ollie?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd tell them we're moving to Plan B and nobody's in trouble. Ollie is eleven and he'd be fine with that, Zara would want details. I'd give her some, like we're saving for the mortgage, and I'd ask her to help me with the salon side project's Instagram.

say: I'd say it's going to be messy and fast, and people need to **prepare**.
I'd tell colleagues that being good with the tools won't be **enough**.
I'd say governments should talk about **income support** now, not in 2028.

S2.quote: A salon manager job could keep me in beauty until 2031 or so, but it's a bridge, not a place to live.
fieldNote: Alarm turns into **action**; she lists three moves and starts them at once.

steps.text: Build the side business for independent salons into paid work

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2034. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say five years is the best case of the three fast ones, and we should use it. At work I'd run a lunchtime session on the tools. Online I'd say, retrain now, don't wait for the headline.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I think I get a few good years. I'm adaptive, I'll be early on each tool, and that earns me time. But 2031 is 2031. I'd want to be out of pure buying and into something with people by then.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd start the side business properly in year one, aim for twenty salon clients and about eight hundred a month. I'd put that toward a six-month cushion. And I'd do a business course, evenings, since I'd need the books and the legal basics.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Motivated, with a bit of fear underneath. It's like having a new project at work, which I like, but with real stakes.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you need to see to decide to leave Lumen?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: If my side income got to about two-thirds of my pay, or if Lumen froze hiring for buyers, whichever came first. I'd rather leave a year early than a year late. At two years I'd have to jump, and at five I get to choose.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you do about Dev's lumpy income in the meantime?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd ask him to build a rainy-day pot with me, and sign up for a regular maintenance contract for local landlords, so there's a steady base. He resists it because he likes being free, but he sees my point.

I'd run a lunchtime session on the tools at **work**.
I'd say retrain now, don't wait for the **headline**.
think: I get a few good years because I'm early on each **tool**.

S3.quote: I'd rather leave a year early than a year late.
fieldNote: Sets a **trigger** for leaving: side income at two-thirds of pay, or a hiring freeze.
Prefers leaving early to **leaving late**; time lets her choose.
Wants her partner to build a **steady base** of contracts, a gentle push he resists.

steps.text: Grow the salon side business to twenty clients in year one
Put the side income toward a six-month cushion
Take an evening business course on books and legal basics

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: This one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any thinking work a person can do. Robots that can do hands-on work as well as people come about 3 years later, around 2039. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years is a long runway, so I'd tell people to stay curious and keep one foot in new tools. I'd share articles with my team and see who's interested. I wouldn't panic anyone.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Privately I feel pretty good. By 2036 I'd be fifty-three, the kids grown, and I'd have a decade to build something. The risk is I get comfortable at Lumen and miss the right moment to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep learning, aim for senior buyer in three years, which means a pay rise. I'd save most of it and put a bit into an index fund, so we get to six months. I'd build the side business slowly. And I'd help Zara choose a degree that's not just desk work, maybe design or nursing.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm, mostly, and a little excited. Ten years feels like a long project, not a countdown. I'd still check the news each week though.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would make this feel less calm?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: A big group buying Lumen, which can happen in a flat market. That could cost me my job in two years, long before AGI. So I keep my network warm and my side income going.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What kind of degree would you steer Zara toward?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Something where she'd work with people, or make things, like design, nursing or teaching. I'd not push her, but I'd say it at dinner a few times. She wants to be a graphic designer, which I'd tell her is fine as long as she learns the AI tools better than anyone.

say: I'd say ten years is a long **runway**; stay curious and keep one foot in new tools.
I'd share articles with my team and see who's **interested**.
think: I feel pretty good: I'd be fifty-three with the kids **grown**.
The risk is getting comfortable at Lumen and missing the right moment to **go**.

S4.quote: Ten years feels like a long project, not a countdown.
fieldNote: Ten years feels like a **project**, so her mood is close to calm, tempered by money pressures.
Sees a **takeover** of her firm as a nearer risk than AGI.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one. I'm good with change, but not with change that lands on a mortgage with no savings. What would help is a safety net that works fast, like income support while I build my own thing, and a bit of help for small businesses like the salons I'd work with.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: Only that being good with new tools isn't the same as being safe. I'd like people to hear that from someone who uses them every day.

headlineQuote: Being good with new tools isn't the same as being safe.
portrait: Chloe is a **43-year-old** junior buyer at a beauty wholesaler, with a self-employed electrician partner and two kids.
She is a pragmatic centrist and uses AI **every day**, moving early on each new tool.
Her skill is both armour and risk, so she builds a **side business** for independent salons.
With under a month saved, she is uneasy at best and **alarmed** if AGI arrives in 2028.
biggestWorry: The 2028 case, because change landing on a mortgage with **no savings** leaves no room to build.
whatWouldHelp: A fast **safety net**, income support while she builds her own business, and help for small salons.
